text:
Chapter Thirty-Three


“Ican’t believe she…” Rory started, but Arthur stopped him with a single hand in the air and a resigned glare. He didn’t want to hear it. He didn’t want to say anything bad about Maggie or listen to his brother defend him. “You didn’t deserve…”


“Ror, stop. I knew what I agreed to.” They had been circling the same thoughts for hours now, and Arthur was sick of it. If there was one thing that was true, it was that Arthur deserved some of this. He’d pushed Maggie too hard. He’d pushed her away, without even realizing it, for months before Beltane. He’d ignored what she’d wanted at every turn. He’d been so lost in his own head, in his own mess, that he had barely stopped to consider what this was like for her. What going to the dean would mean for her. Maggie, whose entire life had been upended by a man who was supposed to love her. He more than deserved her anger.


But he didn’t understand why she seemed to think their breakup was a foregone conclusion. And if she’d been so certain of it, why did she agree to go to dinner with him in the first place? His heart had soared with stupid hope when she’d suggested it, and look where he’d ended up.


Rory looked very much like he had more things that he wanted to say, but he took another swig of his beer and sat back on the sagging old couch. Saturday’s trip to the beach, the baseball game, dinner, they all seemed so far away now. After he left Maggie in their office, he had gone to the library to try to distract himself with work, though he failed spectacularly. And when he finally returned to Atlantia, long after dark, he’d been grateful to find the bungalow empty except for Barry, asleep in his recliner. He’d gone straight to his room, barely bothering to change his clothes, and tossed and turned in his tiny bed until sleep claimed him sometime in the early hours of the morning, when the sky was already starting to lighten.


He didn’t return to Hawthorn the next day, instead letting himself sleep until noon. By then, Barry had already called Rory and told him to come straight over because there was something wrong with Arthur. Rory was waiting for him at the kitchen table with a steaming cup of coffee, a bagel, and an overly concerned look that made Arthur want to turn around and go back to bed. Rory had tiptoed around it all day, but after he put Simon to bed in his old room, he’d cracked open two cans of beer and demanded that Arthur tell him what happened.


“Fuck,” Rory huffed. That sentiment, at least, Arthur was on board with.


He hated this. He hated the pain in his chest, an agonizing ache that he couldn’t ignore. He hated the man who had broken Maggie so thoroughly that she had ended things with Arthur before they had a chance to become something worth fighting for. He hated himself for going to the dean, for ignoring what Maggie wanted. Most of all, he hated himself for believing, like a fool, that he ever could have changed her mind.


“I fucked up, Ror, and I don’t think I can fix it.” He waited for Rory to tell him it wasn’t his fault, that he hadn’t really done anything wrong, but instead, Rory was pulling the soggy label off his beer bottle.


“Did you try?”


“The last time I tried to fix something, it backfired.”


“Did you try to fix it her way?” Arthur looked over at his brother. “Look, you’re used to people like that dean bending over backwards to keep you happy. You’re used to things going your way.”


Arthur felt a pang of shame at his brother’s words, knowing that his life had been easy in a way that Rory’s, that Maggie’s, hadn’t. “I know you thought you did the right thing, made her life easier, but you didn’t,” Rory went on, delivering a hard truth the way only a brother can. “Did you even apologize?”


Had he? He’d been so certain he had. But when he thought back to their conversation, he knew he hadn’t. He had been so afraid of what she was going to say, so upset that she was throwing away what they had, and so worried that she didn’t really feel the same way about him that he never even told her how sorry he was for ruining it all in the first place.


He tilted his head back and finished the rest of his beer. Rory gave him another. And then another. Until, eventually, it was enough to dull the pain.



—


It was only thanks to a piercing banshee screech that Maggie was finally able to persuade Dahlia to go home.


“I told you, I’m fine,” Maggie said again, and just like every other time before, Dahlia pursed her lips and narrowed her eyes. “You can’t stay here forever.”


“Watch me.” Dahlia tucked a crocheted blanket under her chin, snuggling beneath its warmth. She didn’t know it was the one that Maggie kept on the back of her couch because Arthur liked it best. Maggie wanted to fold it and tuck it into a dark corner of the linen closet so she didn’t have to look at it, but that wasn’t something a person claiming to be just fine would do.


“You’ve been here for two days,” Maggie went on.


“And you’ve locked your emotions away someplace where you can’t feel them,” Dahlia argued. “I would leave if you’d just process.” She waved her hands theatrically around the word process.


Maggie sighed. After Arthur had left their shared office, the ghost of their last kiss still on her lips, Maggie had swallowed her sobs and wiped away her tears until her cheeks burned. She had done her best to reason away her sorrow, reminding herself—and later Dahlia—that this was always how the summer was going to end.


“You should go home before it gets dark,” Maggie said. “If I start processing, I promise I’ll call you.”


Another banshee’s cry echoed through the Wilds, and Dahlia looked out at the dusky sky. “You swear?” she asked, turning her worried expression back to Maggie.


“Cross my heart.” Maggie dramatically dragged her fingers over her chest in an X.


She only had to reassure Dahlia four more times before her friend finally left, but not before Dahlia gave her a long, squeezing hug that almost threatened to unwind Maggie’s grief.


When she was alone, every stupid little thing in her apartment reminded her of Arthur. A Tarot Team mug he always chose because the handle was wide enough for his hand. The blue ceramic plate she’d emptied for him to rest his watch and glasses on at night. The stack of books he’d left on her dining room table thinking he’d be back. His tweed jacket, hanging on a hook on the back of her door.


Their lives were never supposed to intertwine like this. Their break was supposed to be the easy part, but instead he had set down roots around her, and she needed to dig them out. She found a large cardboard box and began placing each item that reminded her of Arthur inside, starting with the blanket and ending with his jacket. She left it by the door to take to campus in the morning.


Later, she was wrung out and exhausted, sleep just out of reach. She longed to disappear into oblivion for a few hours, but instead she tossed and turned, her legs twisting in her sheets. When she felt the first hint of an aching grief that she wasn’t ready to confront, she instead clung to her anger like a life raft.


It was easy enough to conjure the shame she’d felt in her office as Dean Clearwater interrogated her about how she had persuaded Arthur to part with his money to fund the grant. It was easy to drag to the surface her frustration at Arthur and the way he always thought he knew what was best for her. But as angry as she was at him, she was even angrier at herself. She was supposed to know better. She could have put a stop to this in June and saved them both so much grief, but now it was mid-July, and she had broken both of their hearts.


Hours passed this way as she alternated between her anger and her resignation. When she heard the first notes of birdsong announcing the coming dawn, she groaned and twisted again, burying her face in her pillow only to realize it smelled like Arthur’s shampoo. She ripped the pillowcase off and rolled ungracefully out of bed, stomping out of her room to the washing machine in the hall. She threw it in with all the force of her pent-up frustration and then slid down to the floor, her back against the cool metal. Gods below, she just wanted to sleep.


At first, she thought the strange undulation of the pool of moonlight at the end of the hall was a trick of her exhaustion. It rippled and flashed a lavender color that she knew all too well, and suddenly Maggie was wide awake. She scrambled to her feet and followed the light to the large windows in her living room that faced Hawthorn. Above the line of trees that separated campus from her apartment property, she saw a hazy purple glow that must have come directly from Ilex Hall.


“What is that?” she said to no one, her fingers grazing the glass.


There was a low rumble, a brightening of the haze, and then the ground itself began to tremble. Her blinds tapped against the window, and glasses in her cabinets clinked together. Maggie had been in plenty of small earthquakes out west, and that was exactly what this felt like, but Galloway didn’t have earthquakes.


Maggie’s heartbeat quickened as she swore and lifted her window. Immediately the smell of burnt ether was overwhelming, singeing her throat. She sputtered and coughed before slamming the window back down, but it did nothing to dissipate the foul odor. Whatever was happening at Ilex Hall, whatever was happening to the pall…Above and below, they were all in danger.


She tripped over her own feet as she ran back to her bedroom, knocking her knee against the door as she reached for her phone. She knew she should alert the wardsmiths first, but there was only one person she wanted by her side right now. There was always only one person she was going to call.



—


It took Arthur a moment to realize that the horrible, insistent buzzing sound wasn’t coming from the inside of his head. He wasn’t sure what it was that had finally cut through the hazy fog that surrounded his brain, but something had woken him up and made him aware of his pounding headache. He groaned, fumbling for his glasses on the nightstand, when his hand hit his phone, buzzing relentlessly. He flipped it open and held it close to his face so he could see the words flashing across the screen: Maggie Linden, PhD. “Fuck,” he said, hitting the answer button.


“Maggie?” he rasped, his voice scratchy and unused.


She was frantic. “Where are you? Why haven’t you been answering your phone?”


“I’m in bed, Maggie.” For the first time, he felt angry at her. She may be able to just shake off the weeks they’d spent together, but he couldn’t. Wouldn’t. But the anger faded when he heard the unmistakable screech of a banshee in the background, far closer than it should have been.


“I’ve been calling you for hours. You need to get to Hawthorn right now. It’s the pall.”


“What happened?” Finally, he found his glasses and the room came into focus as he searched for pants and a shirt.


“I don’t know.” Her voice trembled, and he hated how far away he was, with every thought clouded by fog. He was exhausted. Spent. “I was at home and the ground shook. There was a loud crack that sounded like it was right outside my window, but it came from Ilex Hall.”


“Shit,” Arthur cursed. “The decoction isn’t ready.” He threw his keys into his pocket, put his hand over the receiver, and yelled down the hallway. “Ror!”


“It has to be. Dr. Silva said that it has reached ninety-eight percent efficacy, and we’re going to have to take our chances. How soon can you get here? I called the wardsmith, but…” She hesitated. “I need you here, Arthur.”


Arthur’s brain was too foggy with exhaustion and panic to feel anything about what she said. He flipped his wrist around to look at his watch. It was seven in the morning, so there wouldn’t be much traffic. He could do it in thirty-five minutes if he hurried. After he told Maggie, she said, “I’ll wait for you under the hawthorn.” And then she hung up the phone.


“Ror!” Arthur called again. Gods below, where was his brother? Finally, Rory stuck his head inside the front screen door, looking remarkably alert for someone who had stayed up just as late as Arthur and had just as many beers. “Do you have work today?”


“No, I’m working this weekend.”


“Is Pop or Lane around? Can they watch Simon?” Simon, always an early riser, was drawing on the sidewalk out front with chalk, covering everything in fake runes and shouting nonsense Diadhan spells.


“Mom’s watching him later today anyway. We just need to walk over. What happened?”


“There’s an emergency at the school, and I need you to come with me. I’ll explain on the way there.” He was already jumping into his truck while Rory scooped up Simon without hesitation.


“Special treat! We get to ride in the back!” He deposited Simon over the side of the truck bed and then hopped in, hitting the cab so Arthur knew he could start driving. Lane’s house was only two blocks away, but he still drove at a snail’s pace until he arrived at the bungalow that looked remarkably like his father’s, except its garden beds were beautifully manicured with an assortment of colorful flowers. The collection of discarded baseballs and lawn toys was exactly the same, though. Rory dropped Simon off in record time, waving to Lane, who stood watching her son leave from the front porch, and then climbed back into the cab. When they finally got onto the marshy road that connected Atlantia and Galloway, Arthur began to tell Rory everything.


By the time they were halfway to Hawthorn, Rory was yelling. “Above and below, Artie, why the fuck didn’t you tell anyone about the pall?”


“I didn’t want you to worry.”


“For months! You’ve been trying to solve this on your own when…”


“I’ve had Maggie,” he said feebly. “I didn’t want anyone else to get hurt.” Rory shook his head, staring out the window with a hard set to his jaw.


The closer they got to Hawthorn, the darker the sky became. Atlantia’s summer-blue, sunny weather turned into a biting fall gloom, with low-hanging dark clouds and a misty rain that was cold enough to chill. Arthur cursed. For months, the changes to the weather had been contained to the one mile around the school, but here they were, still ten miles away, and it looked like a dreary November evening.


“Has it been this bad?” Rory asked, and Arthur just shook his head.


Whatever fog had lingered in his brain thanks to his hangover was gone as he and Rory jogged around Ilex Hall toward the hawthorn tree. Maggie was where she promised she’d be, her hair damp and sticking to her forehead. Dahlia and Dr. Silva were with her, pouring the gloaming creeper decoction into a vat of paint. The mixture was a deep, rich purple, but he knew it should have had at least another twelve hours to settle before they used it. He hoped it would be enough to reverse the pall.


Outside of Ilex Hall, it was clear that the situation inside had deteriorated. The lights inside the entire building were blinking, casting eerie shadows on the lawn, and wispy wraiths were skating around the edges of the light. A few bricks had come dislodged from Ilex Hall’s facade and scattered on the lawn where they’d fallen. On the third floor, clouds of lavender pall pressed up against the windows so hard, Arthur was afraid they might shatter, taking out the runes he’d carefully redrawn with Maggie after graduation. If this monstrous pall got out…he didn’t want to think about what would happen.


When Maggie looked up from the paint and noticed him coming toward them, all he could see was her relief. Her shoulders sagged, and her hand came up to her chest. Her eyes were red and puffy, like she’d been crying, and all he wanted to do was go to her and stand next to her, to envelop her in an embrace that would reassure her. Instead, he stayed on the other side of the picnic table even though it killed him.


“I brought Rory to help out,” he said, as if that weren’t obvious. Rory was already next to Dahlia, holding empty paint pens while Dahlia filled them carefully.


Maggie nodded absentmindedly. “Jim is here, too. He’s getting more supplies and then he’s going to stand at the south stair with Dr. Chen as backup. Dahlia was going to stand at the north stair door after we go in. Can Rory stay with her?”


“Of course,” Rory said.


There was so much Arthur wanted to say. He needed to know if she was okay, if she had eaten, if she had slept. “I’m sorry,” he said, like it was meant for the entire group of people gathered there, but he didn’t go on until Maggie looked at him. “I’m sorry I didn’t answer my phone right away.” It wasn’t the real thing he wanted to apologize for, but it was an apology she needed to hear all the same.


She just nodded, going back to the clipboard in front of her. When they finished filling the pens a moment later, there was nothing left to wait for. “I’ll stay out here,” Dr. Silva said. “Wardsmiths are on their way, and if we need additional backup, I’ll call for it.”

facts.fact: Atlantia 宿醉：他止住 Rory 的辩护——我签的是什么我清楚；自我清算：推开她太久/无视她要什么。
facts.anchor: I knew what I agreed to

facts.fact: 军师课：你试过用她的方式修吗——你习惯了院长们围你转；最痛一刀：你到底道歉了没有。
facts.anchor: Did you try to fix it her way?

facts.fact: 道歉幻觉：他以为道过歉——回想对话发现自己从没说出口。
Galloway 守灵夜：Dahlia 霸占沙发两天；crocheted 毯子是他最爱的那条——自称 fine 的人不会藏毯子。
物证装箱：马克杯/蓝瓷盘/书堆/tweed——他把根须扎进她的领地，她得挖出来；装箱放门口。
失眠清算：气他更气自己——本可以在六月叫停；枕套香波味逼她洗枕套滑坐地板。
facts.anchor: clung to her anger like a life raft

facts.fact: 凌晨异变：月光池泛 lavender 波纹——窗外 Ilex Hall 紫雾；地面震颤百叶窗敲窗；开窗被 burnt ether 燎喉。
facts.anchor: the ground itself began to tremble

facts.fact: 第一个电话：该先通知 wardsmiths——但只有一个人她要他在身边；I need you here, Arthur。
车程坦白：Rory 炸锅为何瞒几个月——我有 Maggie；我不想任何人受伤；十英里外已是阴郁十一月。
山楂树集结：她眼红鼻肿看见他肩膀垮下来；decoction 灌入 paint 大桶（少 settle 12 小时）；部署：Jim+Chen 南梯/Dahlia 北梯/Rory 随 Dahlia/Silva 外线。
facts.anchor: all he could see was her relief

facts.fact: 他隔着野餐桌说对不起没秒接电话——不是真想道歉的事，但是她需要听的版本。
facts.anchor: I’m sorry I didn’t answer my phone right away
